title: The Last Portrait
premise: Hospice nurse Astrid Delacroix has spent years recording the strange final rituals of the dying, including her grandmother's habit of counting backwards toward a well on the family property. When every photograph in grandma's house begins showing an extra empty chair, Astrid realizes something was invited in decades ago and is now collecting its seat at the table. As the house's former residents appear one by one to confess what they bargained for during a drought long past, Astrid must choose between protecting her brother Tomas with comforting lies or telling him the truth that could break the invitation. She holds out through one terrible night in the house until sunrise, when the well refills and the debt comes due; she survives by offering the truth aloud instead of a life, freeing the bound dead but losing every photograph, every record, and part of her own memory of grandma.
about_author: Quentin Oyelaran is a former night-shift archivist who claims he began writing horror after cataloguing a collection of family photographs that no one could account for. He lives near the coast, where he keeps an unexplained chair in his study that he refuses to discuss.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At the hospice, she documents Mr. Halloran counting backwards from ninety as he dies, each number matching water dripping somewhere in the walls. Her notebook of dying rituals grows by one entry. Emotional beat: professional calm masking a lifetime of unease about numbers and water.

chapters.title: Grandma's House, Empty
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. After the funeral, Astrid and her brother Tomas sort grandma's belongings in the sealed-up house. The well out back is dry, capped with a stone grandma never let anyone touch. Emotional beat: grief tangled with relief at finally being able to leave.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Sorting photographs, Tomas notices a wooden chair in the background of every picture—weddings, christenings, Christmas mornings—in a spot where no chair ever stood. In the newest photos it sits closer to the camera. Emotional beat: creeping wrongness disguised as a sorting error.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid photographs every image in the album to track the chair's movement overnight. The chair advances frame by frame, approaching the table where the family always sat. Emotional beat: her compulsion to record becomes both shield and trap.

chapters.title: What Grandma Never Said
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. In grandma's locked desk, Astrid finds a ledger of payments—flour, coins, blood-typed notes—dated to the drought summer of 1961, all addressed simply 'to the Well.' Emotional beat: betrayal by omission; loyalty to the dead curdling into questions.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers Rain
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Astrid then elderly neighbor Ruth. Ruth recalls the drought: grandma's sister Ada vanished that August, and after that, rain came. The family stopped speaking of Ada entirely. Emotional beat: the first crack in the family's founding silence.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred and Sixty-Three
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. That night Astrid dreams in countdowns and wakes to find every clock in the house stopped at 3:07. The extra chair now appears in photographs taken this week—including one of Astrid sleeping. Emotional beat: the observation has become mutual.

chapters.title: Tomas Wants to Sell
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas, pragmatic and frightened, wants to burn the albums, sell the house, and never return. Astrid refuses; destroying the record feels like abandoning whoever is still owed. Sibling fracture over loyalty versus truth. Emotional beat: love expressed as conflict.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Well Water
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid uncaps the stone against every instinct and finds the dry well lined with photographs—hundreds, face-down, all of Ada. When she lifts one, water sounds begin beneath the house though the well is empty. Emotional beat: awe tipping into dread.

chapters.title: Ada Comes Home
chapters.summary: Ada's POV (a haunting interlude). A fragmentary voice recounts 1961: starving, bargaining, promising 'a seat forever' in exchange for rain, then walking into the well. Emotional beat: pity for the monster; the horror was hunger before it was hunger again.

chapters.title: Invited Guests
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Dead relatives begin appearing politely at dusk, sitting in the extra chair one at a time, each asking Astrid to confirm they are remembered. Refusing to answer makes the chair move closer to hers. Emotional beat: hospitality weaponized.

chapters.title: Ruth's Warning
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth reveals the town knew: families that thrived in the drought had all made the same bargain, and the well 'refills' every generation to collect. Sunrise is the only safe hour. Emotional beat: communal guilt; survival built on buried debts.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Last Page
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The final ledger page lists not payment but inheritance: 'the seat passes to the rememberer.' Astrid understands the chair has been waiting for whoever keeps the records—her. Emotional beat: the price of being the family's witness.

chapters.title: Burning the Evidence
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas burns the albums while Astrid sleeps; by morning the photographs are intact, ash-scented, and the chair now stands beside his bed too. The house will not let them divide the debt. Emotional beat: futility of denial; forced partnership.

chapters.title: One Night Until the Well Refills
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Rain forecast for dawn—the well refills with the season's first storm. The relatives gather at the table, patient, and set two more places: for Astrid and Tomas. Emotional beat: siege atmosphere; tenderness between siblings under pressure.

chapters.title: The Longest Hour
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Past midnight, the house counts backwards aloud in grandma's voice. Each relative tells their confession in turn, and the truth of 1961 assembles itself piece by piece. Emotional beat: dread transformed into testimony.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid realizes the entity isn't Ada—it's the thing Ada bargained with, wearing her shape, kept fed by sixty years of polite silence. The silence itself was the invitation renewed at every withheld truth. Emotional beat: revelation as responsibility.

chapters.title: Tomas Runs
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas breaks for the door at 4 a.m.; the hallway returns him to the kitchen without his having turned around. He comes back to the table and takes Astrid's hand. Emotional beat: cowardice confessed, courage chosen.

chapters.title: The Truth Out Loud
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At the table, Astrid speaks the whole truth—Ada's starvation, the family's complicity, her own years of documenting instead of intervening—and offers the confession in place of a life. The chair empties. Emotional beat: truth as sacrifice and ransom.

chapters.title: Sunrise and the Refilling Well
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Rain arrives with dawn; the well fills with clean water. The relatives fade mid-gesture, freed, and Ada's photograph surfaces face-up at last. The extra chair remains, ordinary wood, holding nothing. Emotional beat: exhausted, hard-won peace.

chapters.title: What the Records Cost
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Every photograph of grandma is blank now, and Astrid can no longer recall her grandmother's voice—payment taken from the rememberer. She writes down everything she still can before it goes. Emotional beat: mourning the price of survival.

chapters.title: The Chair I Keep
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Astrid's POV. Months later, Astrid works hospice nights again, still counting with the dying—but now she answers them aloud, truthfully, so nothing waits unspoken. In her apartment there is one extra chair, and she leaves it empty on purpose, as a promise kept rather than a debt owed. Emotional beat: scarred but deliberate hope.
